annotation_description: Playing Urza's Saga before Ifnir Deadlands means the player must crack Prismatic Vista this turn to produce {B} for Thoughtseize, wasting the fetch land early. Ifnir Deadlands would have provided {B} immediately (at 1 life) while preserving Prismatic Vista for a future turn when it could be more valuable.

Phlage is a strong card but it requires escape cost (RRWW + exile 5 cards from graveyard), meaning it won't come back easily. Meanwhile, Leyline Binding with Leyline of the Guildpact on the battlefield costs only W (since all lands are every basic type, giving 5 domain), and it can exile any nonland permanent including Urza's Saga or Nethergoyf. Leyline Binding is essentially a 1-mana removal spell that could answer any threat Haiku Coach deploys. Stubborn Denial is also worth considering since with a 4+ power creature (Territorial Kavu with domain or Nethergoyf), it becomes a hard counter that could protect key permanents or counter Kozilek's Command.

Gem3F Johnny has Stubborn Denial in hand and Arid Mesa on the battlefield with Leyline of the Guildpact (making Arid Mesa every basic land type, so it can tap for any color including blue). Stubborn Denial costs {U} and would counter Thoughtseize (a noncreature spell) unless the opponent pays {1}. The opponent has only a Swamp and Urza's Saga (which on chapter I can only add {C}), and already spent {B} to cast Thoughtseize, so they have no mana available to pay the {1}. This would be a hard counter effectively. Instead, Johnny declined to respond and let Thoughtseize resolve, which will strip one of their important cards (likely Territorial Kavu or Leyline Binding). Countering Thoughtseize with Stubborn Denial would be a clean 1-for-1 trade protecting their entire hand.

With Leyline of the Guildpact on the battlefield, all lands are every basic land type, making Leyline Binding cost just {W} (5 less due to domain). The player has an untapped Arid Mesa that could tap for mana (since it's every basic land type thanks to Leyline of the Guildpact). However, the opponent has no nonland permanents worth exiling right now (Urza's Saga is a land). More importantly, the player should be deploying Territorial Kavu this turn as a 5/5 threat (all 5 basic land types), but they have only 1 land untapped and no Mountain in play yet. They should activate Arid Mesa to fetch a Mountain, then cast Territorial Kavu. By passing without activating Arid Mesa or playing their Mountain from hand, they miss deploying a 5/5 on turn 2.

With Leyline of the Guildpact on the battlefield, all lands are every basic land type, meaning Leyline Binding costs only {W} (5 less due to domain). The player could also activate Arid Mesa to fetch a Mountain (or any land), thinning the deck and enabling revolt for future Fatal Pushes. More importantly, passing without cracking Arid Mesa means missing the opportunity to use that mana efficiently. The player has Territorial Kavu to cast next turn (which would be a 5/5 with Leyline of the Guildpact), but declining to crack Arid Mesa at end of opponent's turn is a small missed optimization - they could crack it now to have two untapped lands next turn while keeping options open.

With Leyline of the Guildpact on the battlefield, all lands are every basic land type, so Mountain would produce all colors of mana just like Steam Vents. Playing Steam Vents costs 2 life to enter untapped (or loses tempo entering tapped) for no additional benefit over the free-to-play Mountain.

Playing Territorial Kavu before combat is generally fine since there's no combat yet on turn 2 going first, but the player should consider whether playing Mountain first (to ensure the land drop) and then Kavu would be better sequencing. More importantly, playing Kavu before playing the Mountain means if they want to hold up Stubborn Denial after playing Mountain, they'd have exactly the mana. However, the real concern is sequencing: playing a creature before combat when holding Stubborn Denial (a trick) isn't relevant here since it's their own turn. The bigger question is whether to play Mountain first before committing the Kavu - if Kavu resolves, they can play Mountain and hold up Stubborn Denial with Ferocious active (Kavu is 5/5 with Leyline making all lands every basic type). Actually, the order doesn't matter much since the opponent is tapped out. This play seems reasonable.

Fatal Push was cast before playing a land for the turn. Haiku Coach had Ifnir Deadlands in hand and 0 land drops used this turn. By playing Ifnir Deadlands first (a Desert), they would have had 3 mana sources available and could still cast Fatal Push. More importantly, if they had played Prismatic Vista earlier or had a fetchable land, sacrificing a permanent before casting Fatal Push would enable Revolt, allowing it to kill creatures with mana value 4 or less. In this case, Territorial Kavu has MV 2, so Revolt isn't strictly needed for this target, but the sequencing principle of playing lands before spells is still relevant - having the extra mana open after casting the spell could matter for future plays or bluffing.

Casting Leyline Binding before activating Arid Mesa means only 2 mana remains after Binding, not enough for Winternight Stories (costs {2}{U}). Fetching first would provide a 4th land, allowing both Leyline Binding (1 mana with domain) AND Winternight Stories (3 mana) in the same turn.

Haiku Coach declined to cast Fatal Push on Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer during their own precombat main phase. Ragavan is a high-value threat that generates card advantage and Treasure tokens every time it connects. Fatal Push can destroy it (mana value 1, well within the 2-or-less threshold). While waiting until the opponent's combat to cast it is sometimes correct, there's no downside to killing Ragavan now since it's already on the battlefield and the opponent has tapped-out lands. Additionally, Haiku Coach has Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth making all lands Swamps, so they have plenty of black mana available. The 'reasoning' suggests they thought it was the opponent's turn, but it's actually Haiku Coach's own precombat main - this appears to be a misread of the game state. However, Ragavan could also be attacked into with Nethergoyf, so killing it with Push while it could be dealt with in combat is a minor resource waste. The real issue is passing without doing anything when they could have removed a dangerous threat.

That said, Arena of Glory could give haste if used with its exert ability - paying {R}, {T}, exert to add {R}{R}, and if that mana is spent on a creature spell it gains haste. Gem3F Johnny could have cast Ragavan using Arena of Glory's exert ability to give it haste, allowing it to attack this turn and potentially connect for a Treasure token and card exile. Instead, they appear to be casting it with regular mana, missing the haste opportunity. Actually, looking more carefully, the choice is just 'Ragavan' - we don't know which land they tapped. But casting Ragavan in precombat main is correct if they want to attack with it - they'd need haste though. The key question is whether they used Arena of Glory's exert to give haste. Since we can't confirm, and this is a reasonable play regardless (deploying a threat), this is only questionable.

annotation_description: At 6 life facing a Nethergoyf and two Eldrazi Spawn tokens, Gem3F Johnny chose to hard-cast Ragavan for {R} instead of using Dash for {1}{R}. With Dash, if Ragavan is removed, it would return to hand instead of dying. However, hard-casting does leave Ragavan as a permanent blocker, which could be relevant at 6 life - Ragavan could chump-block the Nethergoyf next turn to survive. The trade-off between having a blocker (hard cast) vs. getting immediate attack value and protection from removal (dash) is debatable, but at 6 life with the opponent having a large Nethergoyf, the blocking argument has merit. Still, Dash would give haste for immediate combat damage, potential Treasure + exile, and if opponent has removal Ragavan returns to hand safely.
